claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: The opto-ligand-TCR system is reversible.
claims.source: When we switched PhyBt from the ON to the OFF state by a 1 s pulse of 740 nm light, we stopped the ongoing calcium response initially evoked by PhyBt(660) (Figure 5D), demonstrating that our system is reversible.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observation that 740 nm light can stop the calcium response.

claims.claim: Continuous high intensity (100%) 660 nm light prevented calcium influx when PhyBt(660) was added to the GFP-PIFS-TCR cells.
claims.source: Accordingly, continuous high intensity (100%) 660 nm light prevented calcium influx when PhyBt(660) was added to the GFP-PIFS-TCR cells (Figure 6B, orange line).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: After stopping constant 660 nm illumination, PhyB molecules that were in the ON state were trapped in this state and induced a strong calcium response.
claims.source: After 390 s the constant 660 nm illumination was stopped, so that the PhyB molecules that were in the ON state at this moment were trapped in this state. This allowed them to bind long enough to the TCR and to induce a strong calcium response (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: Constant high intensity 660 nm illumination did not harm the cells.
claims.source: This experiment also demonstrates that the constant high intensity 660 nm illumination did not harm the cells.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that cells could still respond with calcium influx after prolonged illumination.

claims.claim: At 4% and 2% constant 660 nm intensity, calcium influx was evoked.
claims.source: Indeed, at 4% and 2% constant 660 nm intensity, calcium influx was evoked (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: There is a threshold of the PhyB ON half-life in inducing a calcium response that is largely independent of the PhyBt concentration.
claims.source: We observed a threshold of the PhyB ON half-life in inducing a calcium response that was largely independent of the PhyBt concentration, a crucial property of TCR ligand discrimination (McKeithan, 1995) (Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: The threshold half-life was at 3% 660 nm intensity.
claims.source: This threshold half-life was at 3% 660 nm intensity.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text based on the experimental data.

claims.claim: The duration of the ligand-TCR interaction controls calcium signaling.
claims.source: Thus, we were able to control TCR signaling by changing the intensity of continuous 660 nm light, suggesting that the duration of the ligand-TCR interaction controls calcium signaling.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claims.claim: The calcium signal was stopped when illuminating with high intensity continuous 660 nm light (32% and 16%) during an ongoing TCR signal.
claims.source: During this response the long binding events were changed to fast binding events by illuminating with high intensity continuous 660 nm light (32% and 16%). As expected, the calcium signal was stopped, similar as when using 740 nm light (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: The calcium response was not stopped when low intensity continuous 660 nm light (2% and 4%) was used.
claims.source: The calcium response was not stopped when low intensity continuous 660 nm light (2% and 4%) was used, where the half-life of binding is still long.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: The threshold half-life of the PhyBt-GFP-PIFS-TCR interaction to maintain the calcium response was at 3% 660 nm intensity.
claims.source: The threshold half-life of the PhyBt-GFP-PIFS-TCR interaction to maintain the calcium response was again at 3% 660 nm intensity (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Only the model with KPR yielded a satisfactory fit to the PhyBt binding and calcium signaling data.
claims.source: We fitted both mathematical models, the one with and the one without KPR, to the PhyBt binding and calcium signaling data together. Only the model with KPR yielded a satisfactory fit, and a likelihood ratio test, with the absence of KPR being the null hypothesis and the presence of KPR being the alternative hypothesis, showed highly significant support for the KPR model (p<10−6, Figure 7D,E,F and Figure 7—figure supplement 5).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by mathematical modeling and statistical analysis shown in Figure 7D,E,F.

claims.claim: A likelihood ratio test showed highly significant support for the KPR model (p<10−6).
claims.source: We fitted both mathematical models, the one with and the one without KPR, to the PhyBt binding and calcium signaling data together. Only the model with KPR yielded a satisfactory fit, and a likelihood ratio test, with the absence of KPR being the null hypothesis and the presence of KPR being the alternative hypothesis, showed highly significant support for the KPR model (p<10−6, Figure 7D,E,F and Figure 7—figure supplement 5).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: These findings strongly support the existence of KPR at the TCR.
claims.source: Taken together, these findings strongly support the existence of KPR at the TCR.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mathematical modeling and statistical analysis.

claims.claim: The half-life of the PhyB ON-TCR complex varied from 40 s to 2 s over the range of light intensities used.
claims.source: Utilizing the kinetic data, we determined the half-life of the PhyB ON-TCR complex, ln2 /(koff +ki), which varied from 40 s to 2 s over the range of light intensities used (Figure 8C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by mathematical modeling and experimental data shown in Figure 8C.

claims.claim: The threshold half-life of the bivalent PhyBt-TCR interaction (the proofreading duration τKPR) was determined to be 8 s (95% CI: 3 s, 19 s).
claims.source: We determined the threshold half-life of the bivalent PhyBt-TCR interaction, i.e. the proofreading duration τKPR, to be 8 s (95% CI: 3 s, 19 s) (Figure 8D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by mathematical modeling and statistical analysis shown in Figure 8D.

claims.claim: For a threshold half-life of bivalent binding of PhyBt to the TCR complex of 8 s, signaling from the active TCR is half-maximal.
claims.source: Thus, for a threshold half-life of bivalent binding of PhyBt to the TCR complex of 8 s, signaling from the active TCR is half-maximal.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text based on the mathematical modeling results.

claims.claim: The results largely exclude the possibility of fast rebinding events.
claims.source: Furthermore, our results largely exclude the possibility of fast rebinding events, which would have effectively prolonged the half-life of the PhyB ON-TCR complex sensed by a KPR mechanism (Aleksic et al., 2010; Govern et al., 2010) (Appendix 2).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by analysis in Appendix 2.

claims.claim: The opto-ligand-TCR system allows one single ligand-TCR pair to explore a wide range of different binding half-lives when changing the intensity of red light.
claims.source: In conclusion, we engineered the opto-ligand-TCR system, in which one single ligand-TCR pair explores a wide range of different binding half-lives when changing the intensity of red light and in which other parameters of the interaction remain constant, because we have not mutated the binding interface.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement of the experimental system developed in the study.

claims.claim: Other parameters of the interaction remain constant in the opto-ligand-TCR system because the binding interface was not mutated.
claims.source: In conclusion, we engineered the opto-ligand-TCR system, in which one single ligand-TCR pair explores a wide range of different binding half-lives when changing the intensity of red light and in which other parameters of the interaction remain constant, because we have not mutated the binding interface.
claims.evidence: This is a key advantage of the opto-ligand-TCR system stated in the text.

claims.claim: The opto-ligand-TCR system combined with a mathematical model shows that KPR can explain ligand discrimination by T cells.
claims.source: Together with a mathematical model, our data show that KPR can explain ligand discrimination by T cells.
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study stated in the Discussion.

claims.claim: The PhyB-PIF pair enables switching ON and OFF ligand binding in less than a second.
claims.source: Furthermore, using the PhyB-PIF pair enables switching ON and OFF ligand binding (short pulse of 660 and 740 nm light, respectively) in less than a second (Figure 8B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B.

claims.claim: 740 nm light actively disrupts an existing PhyB-PIF interaction, rather than preventing rebinding.
claims.source: Importantly, we show that 740 nm light actively disrupts an existing PhyB-PIF interaction, rather than preventing rebinding.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on the experimental observations.

claims.claim: The light-induced switch between both states and the light intensity-dependent change in the binding dynamics is only found with phytochromes and not with other optogenetic or synthetic systems.
claims.source: Both features, the light-induced switch between both states and the light intensity-dependent change in the binding dynamics, is only found with phytochromes and not with other optogenetic or synthetic systems (Kolar et al., 2018; Smith et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Kolar et al., 2018; Smith et al., 2016).

claims.claim: The opto-ligand-TCR system was able to provoke calcium and Erk MAP kinase signaling.
claims.source: The opto-ligand-TCR system was not only able to provoke calcium and Erk MAP kinase signaling (not shown), but also led to the stimulation of the T cell as measured by the upregulation of the activation marker CD69.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion, with calcium data shown in figures and Erk data mentioned but not shown.

claims.claim: The opto-ligand-TCR system led to the stimulation of the T cell as measured by the upregulation of the activation marker CD69.
claims.source: The opto-ligand-TCR system was not only able to provoke calcium and Erk MAP kinase signaling (not shown), but also led to the stimulation of the T cell as measured by the upregulation of the activation marker CD69.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: The TCR can be fully stimulated in synthetic settings and not only by pMHC.
claims.source: This is in line with systems where other binding domains were fused to the TCR (single chain Fv and DNA, (Minguet et al., 2007; Schamel and Reth, 2012; Taylor et al., 2017), indicating that the TCR can be fully stimulated in synthetic settings and not only by pMHC.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current study and previous work cited (Minguet et al., 2007; Schamel and Reth, 2012; Taylor et al., 2017).

claims.claim: T cells discriminate between ligands due to differences in the ligand-TCR half-lives.
claims.source: Our opto-ligand-TCR system allowed us to show that T cells discriminate between ligands due to differences in the ligand-TCR half-lives (Figure 8), consistent with KPR models (Altan-Bonnet and Germain, 2005; Davis and van der Merwe, 2006; Lever et al., 2016; McKeithan, 1995).
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by experimental data and mathematical modeling shown in Figure 8.

claims.claim: Using the identical ligand-TCR pair for the different half-lives excludes differences in binding geometry, forces or conformational changes as discriminatory parameters.
claims.source: Using the identical ligand-TCR pair for the different half-lives excludes differences in binding geometry (Adams et al., 2011), forces (Kim et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2014) or conformational changes (Gil et al., 2002) as discriminatory parameters in this setup.
claims.evidence: This is a key advantage of the opto-ligand-TCR system stated in the Discussion.

claims.claim: All parameters for the mathematical model are derived using identical conditions in the opto-ligand-TCR system.
claims.source: Furthermore, we measured total binding, the binding kinetics and the activation readout in the same experimental system. Thus, all parameters for the mathematical model are derived using identical conditions.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an advantage of the experimental approach.

claims.claim: Low affinity pMHC, which are non-stimulatory, lead to partial phosphorylation of CD3ζ, whereas high affinity pMHC, which are stimulatory, lead to full phosphorylation of CD3ζ.
claims.source: Low affinity pMHC, which are non-stimulatory, lead to partial phosphorylation, whereas high affinity pMHC, which are stimulatory, lead to full phosphorylation of CD3ζ (Madrenas et al., 1995; van Oers et al., 1993).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Madrenas et al., 1995; van Oers et al., 1993).

claims.claim: Increasing the concentration of low affinity binders did not lead to full CD3ζ phosphorylation.
claims.source: Indeed, increasing the concentration of the low affinity binders did not lead to full CD3ζ phosphorylation (Madrenas et al., 1997), being consistent with KPR.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Madrenas et al., 1997).

claims.claim: Changing the half-life of PhyB ON altered the amount of bound receptors.
claims.source: Interestingly, changing the half-life of PhyB ON and thus the lifetime of the ligand-TCR interaction also altered the amount of bound receptors, and with the help of the mathematical model we could show that the half-life was the decisive parameter for the magnitude of T cell stimulation as measured by calcium influx.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on the experimental observations and mathematical modeling.

claims.claim: The half-life was the decisive parameter for the magnitude of T cell stimulation as measured by calcium influx.
claims.source: Interestingly, changing the half-life of PhyB ON and thus the lifetime of the ligand-TCR interaction also altered the amount of bound receptors, and with the help of the mathematical model we could show that the half-life was the decisive parameter for the magnitude of T cell stimulation as measured by calcium influx.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mathematical modeling and experimental data.

claims.claim: For soluble TCR ligands, bivalent binding is required to trigger the TCR.
claims.source: For soluble TCR ligands, as we have used here, it has been shown that bivalent binding is required to trigger the TCR (Boniface et al., 1998; Cochran et al., 2000; Kaye and Janeway, 1984), possibly due to both a lack of clustering and stabilization of conformational changes of the TCR (Minguet et al., 2007; Schamel et al., 2017; Swamy et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Boniface et al., 1998; Cochran et al., 2000; Kaye and Janeway, 1984; Minguet et al., 2007; Schamel et al., 2017; Swamy et al., 2016).

claims.claim: PhyB monomers did not activate the TCR whereas PhyB tetramers did.
claims.source: Indeed, also in our case PhyB monomers did not activate the TCR whereas PhyB tetramers (PhyBt) did.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: The PhyBt ligands needed to bind for at least 8 s bivalently to stimulate calcium influx.
claims.source: Thus, the PhyBt ligands needed to bind for at least 8 s bivalently, in order to stimulate calcium influx that itself occurred later.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mathematical modeling results.

claims.claim: The KPR duration is not identical to the time delay between ligand binding and calcium influx or other downstream events.
claims.source: Of note, the KPR duration is not identical to the time delay between ligand binding and calcium influx or other downstream events (Figure 9).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and illustrated in Figure 9.

claims.claim: A time delay is a prerequisite for KPR, but does not necessarily indicate that KPR takes place.
claims.source: A time delay is a prerequisite for KPR, but does not necessarily indicate that KPR takes place.
claims.evidence: This is a conceptual clarification stated in the Discussion.

claims.claim: The accompanying paper by Tischer and Weiner found a KPR time of approximately 7 s.
claims.source: In line with our 8 s KPR time, the accompanying paper by Tischer and Weiner found a KPR time of approximately 7 s (Tischer and Weiner, 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the accompanying paper (Tischer and Weiner, 2019).

claims.claim: Independent of the readout and exact design of the optogenetic system, Jurkat cells have a TCR/chimeric antigen receptor based KPR time of 7–8 s.
claims.source: Thus, independent of the readout and exact design of the optogenetic system Jurkat cells have a TCR/-chimeric antigen receptor based KPR time of 7–8 s.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the current study with the Tischer and Weiner study.

claims.claim: Most other studies have calculated a KPR time of between 1–5 s.
claims.source: Most other studies have calculated a KPR time of between 1–5 s (Aleksic et al., 2010; Altan-Bonnet and Germain, 2005; Daniels et al., 2006; Govern et al., 2010; Holler and Kranz, 2003; Kersh et al., 1998) and the time delay between ligand binding and calcium influx was 7 s in one study (Huse et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Aleksic et al., 2010; Altan-Bonnet and Germain, 2005; Daniels et al., 2006; Govern et al., 2010; Holler and Kranz, 2003; Kersh et al., 1998; Huse et al., 2007).

claims.claim: The co-receptors CD4 and CD8 increase the speed of signaling, most likely by efficiently recruiting the kinase Lck to the TCR.
claims.source: In contrast to those studies, our and the Tischer/Weiner systems lack the co-receptor CD4 and CD8 that have been shown to increase the speed of signaling, most likely by efficiently recruiting the kinase Lck to the TCR (Artyomov et al., 2010; Holler and Kranz, 2003; Veillette et al., 1988).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Artyomov et al., 2010; Holler and Kranz, 2003; Veillette et al., 1988).

claims.claim: Differences in the cellular background might contribute to differences in the KPR time.
claims.source: Differences in the cellular background (primary murine T cells versus the human T cell line Jurkat) might also contribute to differences in the KPR time, e.g., if the concentration of kinases or phosphatases was different (Altan-Bonnet and Germain, 2005).
claims.evidence: This is speculation stated in the Discussion, with a citation to support the general concept (Altan-Bonnet and Germain, 2005).

claims.claim: Individual binding events longer than the threshold half-life might be the ones that triggered T cell activation.
claims.source: The half-life of the interaction is a population average over many binding events. Thus, it might be that individual binding events longer than the threshold half-life (8 s in our case) are the ones that triggered T cell activation, as suggested recently (Lin et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is speculation stated in the Discussion, with a citation to support the idea (Lin et al., 2019).

claims.claim: The on-rate in the opto-ligand-TCR system seems to be too slow to significantly contribute to fast rebinding effects.
claims.source: However, the on-rate in our opto-ligand-TCR system seems to be too slow to significantly contribute to this effect (Appendix 2).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by analysis in Appendix 2.

claims.claim: The rate of converting PhyB from ON to OFF is the same for free PhyB and PIF-bound PhyB.
claims.source: In support of the model (Figure 7A), we experimentally demonstrated that the rate of converting PhyB from ON to OFF is the same for free PhyB and PIF-bound PhyB (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: PhyB molecules convert to OFF while being bound to PIF and thereby the PhyB-PIF interaction is lost.
claims.source: These data imply that PhyB molecules also convert to OFF while being bound to PIF and thereby the PhyB-PIF interaction is lost.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: The effective off-rate and binding affinity of PhyB ON to the TCR are light-dependent.
claims.source: Hence, the effective off-rate and binding affinity of PhyB ON to the TCR are also light-dependent (Figure 7B,C).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model and experimental observations, illustrated in Figure 7B,C.

claims.claim: The amount of TCR-bound PhyB decreases with increasing light intensity.
claims.source: Taken together, the model predicts that the amount of TCR-bound PhyB decreases with increasing light intensity, which we confirmed experimentally (Figure 7—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: The change of PhyB ON affinity is a straightforward consequence of the light-controlled PhyB ON half-life.
claims.source: Importantly, the change of PhyB ON affinity is a straightforward consequence of the light-controlled PhyB ON half-life (this contrasts with mutated pMHC ligands (Altan-Bonnet and Germain, 2005; Daniels et al., 2006; Davis and van der Merwe, 2006; Holler and Kranz, 2003; Lever et al., 2016), where affinity changes can be brought about by changes in both on- and off-rates, and potentially other parameters such as orientation of binding (Adams et al., 2011)).
claims.evidence: This is a key advantage of the opto-ligand-TCR system stated in the Results, contrasting it with previous approaches.

claims.claim: Bivalent binding is required to activate the TCR when using soluble TCR ligands.
claims.source: We used a soluble TCR ligand for which - in case of antibodies or pMHC - it was shown that bivalent binding is required to activate the TCR (Boniface et al., 1998; Cochran et al., 2000; Kaye and Janeway, 1984; Minguet et al., 2007), and this most likely was also the case for our opto-ligand-TCR system (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work and data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: The KPR duration in the opto-ligand-TCR system is the time from bivalent binding to the completion of the biochemical signaling steps.
claims.source: Thus, the KPR duration in our system is the time from bivalent binding to the completion of the biochemical signaling steps (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results and illustrated in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

results.result: The authors successfully produced functional PhyB protein that binds to PIF variants. After illumination with 660 nm light, 70% of PhyB molecules complexed with MBP-PIF(wt), and all tested PIF mutants formed similar complexes with PhyB(660). Given that only 80% of PhyB molecules are in the ON state at photoequilibrium, the authors conclude that the majority of PhyB molecules were functionally active.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C19 and C22 provide converging biochemical evidence from size-exclusion chromatography demonstrating functional PhyB-PIF interaction. The 70% complexation compared to the 80% theoretical maximum supports the conclusion that most PhyB molecules are active. The data are internally consistent and appropriately controlled.

results.result: The authors found that PIF(SSA)-TCR (termed PIFS-TCR) showed the highest surface expression among PIF-TCR constructs, but surprisingly, no PhyBt binding to PIFS-TCR on Jurkat cells could be detected despite functional TCR expression (demonstrated by antibody-mediated calcium flux). The authors conclude that PIFS loses its PhyB-binding capacity when fused to TCR and exposed on the T cell surface.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C27 describe a well-controlled negative result. The PIFS-TCR is expressed on the surface (C23), functional when cross-linked with antibody (C25), and PIFS binds PhyB in solution (from earlier claims), yet PhyBt(660) does not bind to cells (C24, C26). This supports the conclusion that surface presentation disrupts binding (C27). Appropriate controls are included.

results.result: The authors engineered GFP-PIFS-TCR constructs with different furin cleavage sites to test whether GFP presence is required for PhyB binding. Constructs with efficient GFP cleavage (F1, F2) showed minimal PhyBt(660) binding, while permanent GFP fusion (noF) resulted in strong light-dependent PhyBt binding. The authors conclude that moxGFP must be present at the cell surface for PIFS to bind PhyBt(660).
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C31 describe a systematic structure-function analysis with appropriate controls. The correlation between GFP retention and PhyBt binding is clear from the data in Figures 4E,F. The intermediate binding with partial cleavage (F3) strengthens the conclusion. The inference that GFP is required for binding is well-supported by the experimental design.

results.result: The authors demonstrate that the GFP-PIFS-TCR system induces TCR signaling and T cell activation in a light-dependent manner. PhyBt(660), but not PhyBt(740), induced strong calcium influx similar to anti-TCR antibody stimulation. Multiple controls confirmed specificity: light alone, cells without GFP-PIFS-TCR, and PhyB monomers did not induce signaling. Bead-coupled PhyBt(660) upregulated the activation marker CD69.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C37 provide comprehensive evidence for functional TCR signaling through the opto-ligand system. The data include appropriate negative controls (C33-C35), multiple readouts (calcium flux and CD69 upregulation), and demonstrate light-dependent specificity. The requirement for tetrameric PhyB (C35) is consistent with prior literature on soluble TCR ligands.

results.result: The authors demonstrate that the opto-ligand-TCR system is reversible: a 1 s pulse of 740 nm light stopped the ongoing calcium response initially evoked by PhyBt(660).
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C39 demonstrate reversibility with clear experimental data (Figure 5D). The ability to terminate an ongoing response with 740 nm light is a key feature of the system and is well-documented. This is an important control demonstrating that the system can be actively switched OFF.

results.result: The authors show that continuous high intensity (100%) 660 nm light prevented calcium influx when PhyBt(660) was added, but stopping the illumination after 390 s allowed PhyB molecules in the ON state to bind long enough to induce a strong calcium response. This demonstrates that constant high intensity illumination does not harm cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C42 describe a clever experiment demonstrating that high intensity 660 nm light prevents signaling by rapid cycling, but cells remain viable and responsive. The recovery of calcium response after stopping illumination (C41) provides strong evidence that cells are not damaged (C42). The experimental design is sound.

results.result: The authors demonstrate that lowering 660 nm light intensity to 4% and 2% evoked calcium influx, and there is a threshold half-life at 3% intensity that is largely independent of PhyBt concentration. This suggests that the duration of ligand-TCR interaction controls calcium signaling.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C46 describe the key experimental observation supporting KPR. The threshold behavior (C44) that is concentration-independent is a hallmark prediction of KPR models. The data in Figure 6C,D support these claims. The inference that binding duration controls signaling (C46) is reasonable given the experimental design.

results.result: The authors show that high intensity continuous 660 nm light (32% and 16%) stopped an ongoing calcium signal, while low intensity light (2% and 4%) did not. The threshold to maintain calcium response was again at 3% 660 nm intensity.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C49 demonstrate that the system can terminate ongoing signaling by shortening binding half-life, complementing the initiation experiments. The consistency of the 3% threshold (C49) with earlier findings (C45) strengthens the overall conclusion. The data are well-controlled.

results.result: The authors fitted mathematical models with and without KPR to the experimental data. Only the KPR model yielded a satisfactory fit, and a likelihood ratio test showed highly significant support for the KPR model (p<10⁻⁶). The authors conclude that these findings strongly support the existence of KPR at the TCR.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C52 describe rigorous statistical model comparison. The likelihood ratio test with p<10⁻⁶ (C51) provides strong quantitative support for KPR over the occupancy model. The conclusion (C52) is appropriately stated given the statistical evidence. However, the model assumptions and parameter identifiability should be carefully considered.

results.result: The authors determined that the half-life of the PhyB ON-TCR complex varied from 40 s to 2 s over the range of light intensities used. The threshold half-life (KPR duration τKPR) was determined to be 8 s (95% CI: 3 s, 19 s), at which signaling from the active TCR is half-maximal.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C55 provide quantitative estimates from the mathematical model fitted to kinetic data. The 8 s KPR time with confidence interval (C54) is a key finding. The wide confidence interval (3-19 s) indicates some uncertainty, but the estimate is reasonable. The interpretation that this represents half-maximal signaling (C55) is consistent with the model.

results.result: The authors conclude that their results largely exclude the possibility of fast rebinding events that would effectively prolong the half-life sensed by KPR.
results.evaluation: Claim C56 is supported by analysis in Appendix 2 (referenced in the text). This addresses an important alternative explanation for apparent KPR. However, the claim is stated as 'largely exclude' rather than definitively, which is appropriately cautious. The supporting analysis should be carefully reviewed.

results.result: The authors conclude that they engineered an opto-ligand-TCR system where one ligand-TCR pair explores different binding half-lives by changing light intensity while keeping other interaction parameters constant (because the binding interface is not mutated). Combined with mathematical modeling, this demonstrates that KPR can explain ligand discrimination by T cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C59 summarize the main achievement and conclusion of the study. The key advantage of the system—varying half-life without changing the binding interface (C58)—is a major strength. The conclusion that KPR explains ligand discrimination (C59) is supported by the combined experimental and modeling evidence, though alternative mechanisms cannot be completely excluded.

results.result: The authors demonstrate that the PhyB-PIF pair enables switching ligand binding ON and OFF in less than a second, and that 740 nm light actively disrupts existing PhyB-PIF interactions rather than just preventing rebinding.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C61 describe important properties of the optogenetic system. The sub-second switching (C60) is supported by Figure 8B. The active disruption by 740 nm light (C61) is an important mechanistic insight supported by the experimental observations, particularly the ability to stop ongoing calcium responses.

results.result: The authors experimentally demonstrated that the rate of converting PhyB from ON to OFF is the same for free PhyB and PIF-bound PhyB, implying that PhyB converts to OFF while bound to PIF, thereby losing the interaction. This makes the effective off-rate and binding affinity light-dependent, and the model prediction that TCR-bound PhyB decreases with increasing light intensity was confirmed experimentally.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C88 describe key mechanistic insights supporting the mathematical model. The experimental demonstration that photoconversion rates are independent of PIF binding (C85, Figure 7—figure supplement 3) is crucial for the model. The confirmation of the predicted decrease in bound PhyB with light intensity (C88, Figure 7—figure supplement 4) validates the model predictions.

results.result: The authors conclude that their opto-ligand-TCR system demonstrates that T cells discriminate between ligands due to differences in ligand-TCR half-lives, consistent with KPR models. Using identical ligand-TCR pairs for different half-lives excludes differences in binding geometry, forces, or conformational changes as discriminatory parameters. All model parameters were derived using identical experimental conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C68 articulate the key advantages of the experimental approach. The ability to vary half-life without changing the binding interface (C67) is a major strength that addresses limitations of previous studies. The unified experimental system (C68) is also an important advantage. The conclusion about half-life discrimination (C66) is well-supported by the data and modeling.

results.result: The authors found that changing the half-life of PhyB ON altered the amount of bound receptors, but mathematical modeling showed that the half-life was the decisive parameter for the magnitude of T cell stimulation as measured by calcium influx.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C72 address an important potential confound: changing half-life also changes receptor occupancy. The mathematical modeling was essential to disentangle these effects and demonstrate that half-life is the decisive parameter (C72). This is a key result supporting KPR over simple occupancy models.

results.result: The authors conclude that bivalent binding is required to activate the TCR with soluble ligands (as PhyB monomers did not activate while tetramers did), and that the KPR duration in their system is the time from bivalent binding to completion of biochemical signaling steps. PhyBt ligands needed to bind for at least 8 s bivalently to stimulate calcium influx.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C75, C90-C91 establish the requirement for bivalent binding, which is well-supported by prior literature (C73, C90) and the current data showing monomers are inactive (C74). The interpretation that KPR time represents bivalent binding duration (C91) is reasonable. The 8 s requirement (C75) follows from the modeling results.

results.result: The authors clarify that the KPR duration is not identical to the time delay between ligand binding and calcium influx or other downstream events. A time delay is a prerequisite for KPR but does not necessarily indicate that KPR takes place.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C77 provide important conceptual clarification distinguishing KPR duration from total signaling time. This is illustrated in Figure 9 and is an important point for interpreting the results. The distinction is conceptually sound and helps avoid confusion.

results.result: The authors note that an accompanying paper by Tischer and Weiner found a KPR time of approximately 7 s, and conclude that independent of the readout and exact optogenetic system design, Jurkat cells have a TCR/chimeric antigen receptor-based KPR time of 7-8 s.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C79 compare results with a companion study using a different optogenetic system. The convergence on 7-8 s KPR time (C79) across different systems strengthens confidence in the findings. However, this is based on citation to another paper, and the generalization should be interpreted cautiously.

results.result: The authors describe the kinetic proofreading (KPR) model, which proposes that T cells discriminate self from foreign ligands by different ligand binding half-lives to the TCR. In KPR, long half-life interactions allow completion of biochemical reactions triggering signaling, while short half-life interactions result in TCR reversion to the inactive state. The authors' mathematical modeling of experimental data showed that ligand-TCR interaction half-life is the decisive factor for activating downstream TCR signaling, substantiating KPR.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C5-C6 describe the KPR model (established theory) and the main conclusion of the study. The description of KPR (C1, C5, C6) is accurate based on the literature. The main conclusion (C3) is supported by the extensive experimental and modeling evidence presented throughout the manuscript. This represents the central finding of the paper.
